2027-02-07.title: Kothine Sunday · First Sunday of the Great Fast
readings: Return to me with all your heart
Is not this the fast that I choose?
In Antioch they were first called Christians
2027-02-07.alt: Kothine Sunday, the miracle at Cana: first Sunday of the Great Fast. The special prayers of the Fast begin this evening; Shubkono, the service of reconciliation, is on Monday 8 February.
2027-02-07.verse: Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
theo: The Malankara Church begins the Great Fast with a wedding. On Kothine Sunday we read the miracle at Cana, where Jesus changed water into wine. It may seem strange to start a season of fasting at a feast, but it is deeply wise. The Fast is not about sadness; it is about transformation. The water of our ordinary, tasteless lives can become the wine of God's joy, if we do what Mary says: “Do whatever he tells you.”

The prophets tell us what kind of fast God wants. Joel: “Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; rend your hearts and not your clothing.” Isaiah: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice… to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” Fasting from food is meant to open our hearts to God and our hands to the poor.

St Paul shows the inner work of Lent: “Put to death whatever in you is earthly… clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience… Above all, clothe yourselves with love.” The Fast is a change of clothes: putting off the old self and putting on Christ. Acts reminds us that it was in Antioch, the mother Church of our Syriac tradition, that the disciples were first called Christians.

The jars at Cana were filled “up to the brim” with water at Jesus' word. In these fifty days, let us fill our jars: with prayer, fasting, almsgiving and the Word of God. At the end of the Fast, at Qyomtho, Christ will give us the best wine, kept until now: the joy of his Resurrection.
conn: At Cana water for purification becomes the wine of the wedding feast; the old covenant is fulfilled in the new (John 2:6–10).
Genesis 9:13: God's covenant after the flood. Lent is a time to return to the covenant God never breaks.
Exodus 20: Lent is a time to examine our lives by the commandments and make a good Confession.
Isaiah 58:6–7 and Joel 2:12–13: fasting with the heart and with the hands.
altar: At Cana Jesus changed water into wine; at the altar he changes wine into his own Blood. Every Holy Qurbono of the Fast is a small Cana, preparing us for the great feast of the Resurrection.
outline: Why does our Lent begin at a wedding?
Water into wine: God changes ordinary lives.
Mary's advice for the whole Fast.
Joel 2 and Isaiah 58: return with the heart, share with the poor.
Prayer, fasting, almsgiving, Scripture; Shubkono and Confession.
live: Decide as a family: one food to fast from, one daily prayer, one work of charity.
Take part in the service of reconciliation on Monday and ask forgiveness of those you have hurt.
Put aside the money saved by fasting for the poor.
fathers: He sings of the Lord who at Cana changed water into wine, and asks him to change our hearts in the same way during the Fast (Hymns on the Fast and on Virginity).
“Do you fast? Give me proof of it by your works… If you see a poor man, take pity on him; if you see an enemy, be reconciled with him” (Homilies on the Statues 3).
magis: Interior penance is expressed in fasting, prayer and almsgiving; Lent is a privileged time for it.
The precept of fasting and abstinence prepares us for the liturgical feasts.
Jesus' presence at Cana confirms the goodness of marriage; the Church sees in it the sign of the new covenant.
saints: 8 Feb (Monday): Shubkono; the Great Fast begins. 10 Feb: anniversary of the establishment of the Syro-Malankara Major Archiepiscopate (2005). 11 Feb: Our Lady of Lourdes, World Day of the Sick.
2027-02-07.prayer: Lord Jesus, at Cana you changed water into wine and revealed your glory. As we begin the Great Fast, change our hearts: teach us to do whatever you tell us, to fast with love, to share with the poor, and to reach with joy the feast of your Resurrection. Amen.

quick: Our Lent begins at a wedding: the Fast is transformation, not sadness.
Mary's advice for Lent: “Do whatever he tells you.”
The fast God chooses: return with the heart, share with the poor.
2027-02-07.action: Make a family Lenten plan: one fast, one prayer, one work of charity.
2027-02-07.question: What water in my life do I want Jesus to change into wine this Lent?
2027-02-07.special: Kothine Sunday, first Sunday of the Great Fast. The special prayers of Lent begin this evening; remind the faithful about fasting and abstinence and about Shubkono on Monday.
illus: In many Malankara homes the meat pots are scrubbed clean on the evening before the Fast, and the family begins fifty days of simpler food. The clean pots are like the jars at Cana: emptied and ready to be filled with something better.

family.explain: At a wedding in Cana the wine ran out. Mary told the servants: “Do whatever Jesus tells you.” Jesus changed water into the best wine! In Lent Jesus wants to change our hearts too.
family.intention: We pray for a holy Lent for our family, and for people who have no food.
family.ask: Ask: “What will each of us give up this Lent, and what good thing will we do?”

kidsaint: His name means “son of encouragement”. In Antioch he encouraged the new Christians, and brought Paul to teach with him; there the disciples were first called Christians. Lesson: encourage others to be good this Lent.
term: Kothine refers to the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11). The Malankara Church begins the Great Fast with this Gospel: the Fast is a time of transformation, from water to wine.
termMore: The service of forgiveness (reconciliation) on the first Monday of the Fast. Priest and people ask forgiveness of one another and of God before beginning the fifty days.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today our Church begins the Great Fast, and it begins it at a wedding. On Kothine Sunday we read how Jesus, at Cana, changed water into wine. Why begin fifty days of fasting with a wedding feast? Because the Fast is not a season of gloom. It is a season of transformation.

At Cana the wine ran out. Mary noticed and said to the servants: “Do whatever he tells you.” That is the best advice for Lent. The servants did a simple thing: they filled the jars with water, up to the brim. And Jesus changed that water into the best wine. In this Fast, let us fill our jars: with prayer, with fasting, with the Word of God, with works of mercy. And let Jesus change the water of our lives into wine.

The prophets tell us what true fasting is. Joel says: “Return to me with all your heart; rend your hearts and not your clothing.” Isaiah says: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” Fasting from food is not a diet; it makes room in our hearts for God and in our hands for the poor.

Tonight the special prayers of the Fast begin, and tomorrow we celebrate Shubkono, when we ask forgiveness of one another. Let each family make a simple plan: one fast, one prayer, one act of charity. And at the end of these fifty days, at Qyomtho, Jesus will give us the best wine, kept until now: the joy of his Resurrection. Amen.
kids: Children, today Lent begins! And our Gospel is about a wedding party. At the party the wine ran out. Mary said: “Do whatever Jesus tells you.”
The servants filled six big jars with water, and Jesus changed it into wonderful wine! In Lent Jesus wants to change us too: to make us kinder, more patient, more prayerful.
What can you give up this Lent? Sweets? Television? And what good thing can you do? Let's say: “Jesus, change my heart!”

intro: Saint Paul speaks of Lent in the language of clothing: take off the old self, put on the new. The Great Fast is the season of changing our garments.

points.h: Put to death what is earthly
sub: Anger, malice, slander.
Lies among one another.
Strip off the old self.
points.apply: Name one sin you will put to death in this Fast and confess it.

sub: Compassion, kindness, humility.
Meekness and patience.
Above all, love.
points.apply: Each morning choose one virtue to wear that day.

points.h: Let the word dwell in you
sub: The word of Christ richly.
Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs.
Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.
points.apply: Read one chapter of a Gospel each day of the Fast.

concl: The Fast is not only giving up food; it is taking off the old self and putting on Christ.
The garment that holds all the others together is love.
opts.resolve: This Fast I will take off one sin, put on one virtue each day, and let the word of Christ dwell in me.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today our Church begins the Great Fast. Saint Paul, in the letter to the Colossians, describes this season with a simple picture: changing our clothes. Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly (Colossians 3:5). And then: you have stripped off the old self with its practices and have clothed yourselves with the new self (Colossians 3:9–10).

What is the old self? Paul names it plainly: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and abusive language. Do not lie to one another (Colossians 3:8–9). These are the old clothes we have worn so long that we no longer notice them. Ezekiel cries out: cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed against me, and get yourselves a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 18:31). The Fast is the time to take them off, and a good confession is where we leave them behind.

Then we must put something on. Empty space does not stay empty. As God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience. Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony (Colossians 3:12, 14). Isaiah sings: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10). Fasting from food is meant to make us kinder, not more irritable.

How is this possible? Paul answers: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16). Moses told Israel to keep God's words in their hearts and to recite them at home and on the road (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). If we feed on the word each day, the new garment will grow on us from within.

So let each of us make a plan today. One sin to take off and confess. One virtue to put on each morning. One chapter of the Gospel each day. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus (Colossians 3:17). Then at Qyomtho we will stand before the risen Lord clothed in his love. Amen.

opts.a: The covenant, the commandments and the name Christian
intro: Today's readings begin with the rainbow, go up to Sinai and end in Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. The Fast is a return to the covenant that makes us who we are.

sub: The bow in the clouds.
God binds himself to his creation.
The new covenant in the blood of Christ.
points.apply: Each time you see the sky this week, thank God for his faithfulness.

sub: God first rescues his people from slavery.
Then he gives the commandments.
Love of God and neighbour fulfils them.
points.apply: Examine your conscience on the Ten Commandments before confession this Fast.

sub: Antioch, a mixed city.
Jews and Greeks together in Christ.
A name we must live up to.
points.apply: Ask yourself each evening: did I live today like a Christian?

concl: God has never broken his covenant; the Fast is our time to return to it.
We bear the name of Christ; the commandments show us how to live worthy of it.
opts.resolve: This Fast I will examine my life on the commandments, make a good confession, and try each day to live worthy of the name Christian.
homily: Dear friends, on this first Sunday of the Great Fast our readings take us on a journey. They begin after the flood, with a rainbow: I have set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth (Genesis 9:13). And God says: I will remember my covenant (Genesis 9:15). Before we make any promise to God, God has already bound himself to us.

Then we go up to Sinai. Notice how the commandments begin: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). God first rescues his people, and only then gives them his law. The commandments are not chains. They are the way a rescued people lives. Jesus gathered them into two: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–39).

That is why the Fast is the right time to examine our lives on the Ten Commandments. Do I give God the first place? Do I keep Sunday holy and come to the Holy Qurbono? Do I honour my parents? Am I honest, faithful and pure? Do I envy what others have? A good examination of conscience prepares a good confession, and a good confession renews the covenant of our Baptism.

Finally the readings take us to Antioch, a great city where Jews and Greeks lived side by side. There the believers lived so differently that the people needed a new word for them: it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). Isaiah had promised: you shall be called by a new name (Isaiah 62:2). Our Syriac tradition has always loved Antioch, the city of that first name.

We bear the same name. The Fast asks us whether people around us can still recognise it in our lives. Jesus says: my sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me (John 10:27). Let us listen to his voice in these fifty days, keep his commandments, and live worthy of the name Christian. Amen.

intro: Theme: “The Fast begins at a wedding.”

Our Great Fast does not begin with ashes but with a wedding at Cana. The Church tells us that Lent is not sadness but the joyful return of the Bride to the Bridegroom, who turns the water of our efforts into the wine of his grace.

sub: Joel calls: return with fasting, weeping and mourning; rend your hearts, not your clothing.
At Cana Mary notices: “They have no wine.” Lent begins by admitting what we lack.
Her counsel is the programme of the Fast: “Do whatever he tells you.”
q: Yet even now, says the LORD, return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; rend your hearts and not your clothing.
When the wine gave out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.” … His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
points.apply: Name the “wine” that has run out in your life (joy, peace, love) and bring it to Jesus.

sub: Fasting from food has meaning when it frees us for justice and charity.
Isaiah: share your bread, shelter the homeless, clothe the naked.
Jesus: fast in secret; the Father who sees in secret will reward you.
q: Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free … Is it not to share your bread with the hungry?
But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that your fasting may be seen not by others but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
points.apply: Set aside the money saved by fasting for the poor.

sub: The servants fill the jars to the brim; Jesus does the rest.
The best wine is kept for last: God's grace exceeds our efforts.
After the flood God gave a covenant sign; at Cana Jesus gives the first sign of the new covenant.
q: I have set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
“You have kept the good wine until now.” Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
points.apply: Fill your “jars” this Lent: daily prayer, Scripture, fasting and charity, and trust Jesus to transform them.

concl: The Fast is a wedding feast in preparation: the Bridegroom is coming to his Passion and Resurrection.
Let us return with all our hearts, fast as God desires, and let him change our water into wine.
2027-02-07.resolve: Choose three Lenten practices (prayer, fasting, almsgiving) and write them down today.
